items.stem: Which of the following best describes "base isolation"?
options: Placing a building on flexible bearings (rubber and steel pads) so that the ground can move without transferring all shaking to the structure
The period after an earthquake within which most trapped survivors can be rescued alive
The UN agreement for 2015-2030 with seven targets and four priorities to reduce disaster deaths, losses and affected people
Using reconstruction to reduce future risk, e.g. safer buildings, better land use and stronger institutions
items.answer: Placing a building on flexible bearings (rubber and steel pads) so that the ground can move without transferring all shaking to the structure
items.markingKey: A. "base isolation" is placing a building on flexible bearings (rubber and steel pads) so that the ground can move without transferring all shaking to the structure.

items.stem: Noah writes: "Earthquake early warning systems predict earthquakes." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They detect earthquakes that have already started and give seconds of warning before strong shaking arrives.
items.markingKey: They detect earthquakes that have already started and give seconds of warning before strong shaking arrives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why prediction is more effective for volcanoes than for earthquakes.
items.answer: Rising magma produces measurable precursors such as harmonic tremor, ground deformation and SO₂ emissions, whereas faults give no reliable short-term warning signs.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rising magma produces measurable precursors such as harmonic tremor, ground deformation and SO₂ emissions, whereas faults give no reliable short-term warning signs. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake had a moment magnitude of 9.1 and the February 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake, Türkiye had a magnitude of 7.8. How many times larger was the ground-motion amplitude of the first earthquake?
items.markingKey: M1 each whole unit = ×10 amplitude; A1 10^1.3 ≈ 20.

items.stem: Briefly describe low-cost housing in Nepal after 2015 and explain what it reveals about low-cost building design.
items.answer: NGOs trained masons in earthquake-resistant techniques such as horizontal timber bands and reinforced corners. Appropriate technology can reduce vulnerability without high costs.
items.markingKey: Context (NGOs trained masons in earthquake-resistant techniques such as horizontal timber bands and reinforced corners.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Appropriate technology can reduce vulnerability without high costs. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to low-cost building design.

items.stem: At a station in Kathmandu, the S-waves from an earthquake arrived 54.5 s after the P-waves. Assuming P-waves travel at 7.0 km/s and S-waves at 4.1 km/s, calculate the distance to the earthquake focus (d = Δt × vp × vs / (vp − vs)). Explain why at least three stations are needed to locate the epicentre.
items.answer: d = 54.5 × 7.0 × 4.1 / (7.0 − 4.1) = 539 km; one station gives only a distance (a circle); circles from three stations intersect at the epicentre (triangulation).
items.markingKey: M1 substitution; A1 539 km. R1 triangulation explained.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim that prediction is more important than preparation in managing volcanic hazards.
items.answer: Prediction is only effective when combined with preparation and trusted communication.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: Pinatubo evacuation saved thousands; monitoring gives warning time. Against / limitations: predictions are uncertain and false alarms cause distrust; preparation (plans, education, zoning) is needed to act on warnings. A supported conclusion might be: Prediction is only effective when combined with preparation and trusted communication. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Data: an early warning station 40 km from an epicentre detects P-waves (6 km/s); S-waves travel at 3.5 km/s. A city lies 120 km from the epicentre.

(a) Calculate the time taken for S-waves to reach the city. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, calculate the warning time for the city if the alert is issued 5 seconds after the P-wave reaches the station. [6]
items.answer: (a) 120 / 3.5 = 34.3 s (b) P arrives at the station at 40/6 = 6.7 s; alert at 11.7 s; warning = 34.3 − 11.7 = 22.6 s
items.markingKey: (a) 120 / 3.5 = 34.3 s (b) P arrives at the station at 40/6 = 6.7 s; alert at 11.7 s; warning = 34.3 − 11.7 = 22.6 s Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). items.stem: ShakeAlert, the earthquake early warning system on the US west coast, works by:
options: detecting P-waves and alerting before damaging waves arrive
items.answer: detecting P-waves and alerting before damaging waves arrive
items.markingKey: A. Warning times are typically seconds to tens of seconds.

items.stem: Explain why hazard mapping is an important pre-event strategy.
items.answer: Mapping identifies zones of high risk (fault traces, liquefaction, lahar and tsunami zones) so planners can restrict building, locate key services safely and design evacuation routes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Mapping identifies zones of high risk (fault traces, liquefaction, lahar and tsunami zones) so planners can restrict building, locate key services safely and design evacuation routes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between prediction and protection.
items.answer: Prediction tries to forecast when and where a hazard will occur so people can be warned; protection reduces damage when it occurs, e.g. by building design or sea walls.
items.markingKey: Prediction tries to forecast when and where a hazard will occur so people can be warned; protection reduces damage when it occurs, e.g. by building design or sea walls. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between new earthquake-resistant buildings and retrofitting existing buildings.
items.answer: New buildings can incorporate designs such as base isolation from the start at relatively low extra cost; retrofitting strengthens existing buildings but is often expensive and disruptive.
items.markingKey: New buildings can incorporate designs such as base isolation from the start at relatively low extra cost; retrofitting strengthens existing buildings but is often expensive and disruptive. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Suggest why hazard maps for volcanoes need regular updating.
items.answer: Vents and lahar paths change after eruptions; settlement expands; new monitoring data improve understanding of hazard zones.
items.markingKey: Vents and lahar paths change after eruptions; settlement expands; new monitoring data improve understanding of hazard zones.

items.stem: Singapore has a population of about 5.9 million and an area of 734 km²; Australia has about 26.6 million people in 7,692,024 km². (a) Calculate the population density of each. (b) How many times more densely populated is the denser country? (c) Explain why national density can hide uneven distribution, using one of these countries.
items.answer: (a) Singapore: 8,038.1 /km²; Australia: 3.5 /km² (b) ≈ 2,324.4 times (c) e.g. most people cluster in favourable areas (coasts, river valleys, cities) while deserts/mountains are almost empty.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 8,038.1, A1 3.5. (b) A1 2,324.4. (c) R1 uneven distribution explained with a physical or human factor.

Study the resource below.

items.answer: Unreinforced masonry is heavy and brittle; modern code concrete and timber are ductile and flex without collapsing.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Rebuilding housing and infrastructure after a disaster, ideally to a higher standard ("build back better")"?
options: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction
items.answer: reconstruction
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of reconstruction.

items.stem: "Recovery is complete once buildings have been rebuilt." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Recovery includes livelihoods, mental health, services and social networks, which can take far longer than rebuilding.
items.markingKey: Recovery includes livelihoods, mental health, services and social networks, which can take far longer than rebuilding. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why recovery from disasters often takes longer in low-income countries.
items.answer: Limited government funds and insurance, dependence on aid that is slow or unco-ordinated, weak institutions, lack of land titles, and damage forming a large share of GDP slow rebuilding. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Limited government funds and insurance, dependence on aid that is slow or unco-ordinated, weak institutions, lack of land titles, and damage forming a large share of GDP slow rebuilding. items.stem: A planner scores two places from 1 (low) to 10 (high) - a village in the Nepal Himalaya: hazard 4, vulnerability 9, capacity 1; a town near Mount Merapi: hazard 9, vulnerability 4, capacity 2. Using risk = hazard × vulnerability / capacity, calculate the risk score for each place and state which has the greater risk.
items.answer: a village in the Nepal Himalaya: 36.0; a town near Mount Merapi: 18.0; greater risk: a village in the Nepal Himalaya
items.markingKey: A1 36.0; A1 18.0; R1 comparison.

items.stem: The 2010 Maule earthquake, Chile (Mw 8.8) caused about 525 deaths in Chile (national population about 17.1 million); the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami (Mw 9.1) caused about 18,500 deaths in Japan (population about 128 million). Calculate deaths per million people for each event. Suggest two reasons for the difference.
items.answer: Chile: 30.7 per million; Japan: 144.5 per million; higher: the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami (Mw 9.1); e.g. building codes and enforcement, poverty and informal construction, preparedness and warning systems, governance and emergency response, depth/distance of the earthquake from population.
items.markingKey: M1 deaths ÷ population (millions); A1 30.7; A1 144.5. R1 R1 two valid, developed reasons.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that international aid is essential for recovery from geophysical disasters in low-income countries.
items.answer: Aid is often necessary but is effective only when it supports local institutions.
items.markingKey: For: funds rebuilding and specialist rescue. Against: can be slow, tied or poorly co-ordinated. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "emergency response".
items.answer: The immediate actions after a disaster to save lives and meet basic needs, such as search and rescue, medical care, shelter, water and food
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the immediate actions after a disaster to save lives and meet basic needs, such as search and rescue, medical care, shelter, water and food. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between international aid and local response.
items.answer: International aid brings money, specialist teams and supplies but may arrive slowly and lack local knowledge; local responders act immediately, know the area and rescue most survivors.
items.markingKey: International aid brings money, specialist teams and supplies but may arrive slowly and lack local knowledge; local responders act immediately, know the area and rescue most survivors. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why "building back better" is difficult to achieve.
items.answer: Pressure to rebuild quickly, cost of higher standards, land disputes, lack of skilled builders and materials, weak enforcement, and communities wanting to rebuild where they lived before.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pressure to rebuild quickly, cost of higher standards, land disputes, lack of skilled builders and materials, weak enforcement, and communities wanting to rebuild where they lived before. items.stem: Suggest why access was a major problem for responders after the 2023 Al Haouz earthquake in Morocco.
items.answer: Remote mountain villages in the High Atlas were reached by narrow roads blocked by landslides and rockfalls, so helicopters and mules were needed.

items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest what City B's curve after one year suggests about its reconstruction. [6]
items.answer: (a) City A suffered a much deeper fall (70 percentage points vs 30) and took four times longer to recover; City B recovered quickly and improved beyond its previous level. (b) It built back better - improved buildings and services raised quality of life above pre-disaster levels.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "insurance"?
options: Insurance that pays out automatically when a measured trigger (e.g. a magnitude or wind speed) is reached, rather than after loss assessment
Strengthening existing buildings, e.g. with steel bracing or shear walls, to resist hazards
A risk-sharing mechanism in which people pay premiums to receive compensation after losses
The period after an earthquake within which most trapped survivors can be rescued alive
items.answer: A risk-sharing mechanism in which people pay premiums to receive compensation after losses
items.markingKey: C. "insurance" is a risk-sharing mechanism in which people pay premiums to receive compensation after losses.

items.stem: Explain the difference between traditional indemnity insurance and parametric insurance.
items.answer: Indemnity insurance pays for assessed losses, which can take months; parametric insurance pays automatically when a trigger is reached, giving fast cash but possibly not matching actual losses.
items.markingKey: Indemnity insurance pays for assessed losses, which can take months; parametric insurance pays automatically when a trigger is reached, giving fast cash but possibly not matching actual losses. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Mei writes: "Insurance reduces the physical damage caused by hazards." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Insurance does not prevent damage; it spreads the financial cost and speeds recovery.
items.markingKey: Insurance does not prevent damage; it spreads the financial cost and speeds recovery. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

Suggest how the place with greater risk could reduce it, other than by changing the hazard.
items.answer: a coastal district of Port-au-Prince: 6.0; a barangay in Tacloban: 2.8; greater risk: a coastal district of Port-au-Prince; reduce vulnerability (building codes, land-use zoning) or increase capacity (warnings, drills, emergency services, insurance).
items.markingKey: A1 6.0; A1 2.8; R1 comparison. R1 strategy targeting vulnerability or capacity.

items.stem: Christchurch's central business district was cordoned off after the 2011 earthquake for about:
items.answer: two years

items.stem: The Caribbean Catastrophe Risk Insurance Facility (CCRIF) is an example of:
items.answer: parametric insurance shared between countries

items.stem: Briefly explain why land-use zoning is often difficult to apply in practice.

items.answer: Resistance is the ability to withstand a hazard without damage; resilience includes the ability to absorb impacts and recover quickly afterwards.

items.stem: "Post-event responses are less effective than pre-event strategies in reducing the impacts of geophysical hazards." Discuss this statement, with reference to examples you have studied.
items.answer: Pre-event strategies are more cost-effective, but effective response and recovery remain essential.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: prevention saves more lives (codes, warnings); every dollar on preparedness saves several in response. Against / limitations: rapid response saves trapped survivors; recovery offers chances to build back better. A supported conclusion might be: Pre-event strategies are more cost-effective, but effective response and recovery remain essential. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Sendai target data: a country recorded 2,400 disaster deaths per year on average in 2005-2015 and 1,560 in 2015-2025.

(a) Calculate the percentage change in average annual deaths. [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, suggest why this measure alone may not show improved resilience. [6]
items.answer: (a) (1,560 − 2,400)/2,400 × 100 = -35.0% (b) Deaths vary with the number and size of events, so a quiet decade may look like improvement; economic losses and numbers affected must also be considered.
items.markingKey: (a) (1,560 − 2,400)/2,400 × 100 = -35.0% (b) Deaths vary with the number and size of events, so a quiet decade may look like improvement; economic losses and numbers affected must also be considered. Credit relevant own knowledge and named examples in (b). items.stem: Evaluate the claim that building design is the most effective way to reduce earthquake risk.
items.answer: Building design is the single most important measure, but it must be enforced and combined with warnings and planning.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: most deaths come from collapse; Japan and Chile show codes work. Against / limitations: useless without enforcement (Türkiye); cannot prevent tsunami deaths; warnings and education also needed. A supported conclusion might be: Building design is the single most important measure, but it must be enforced and combined with warnings and planning. items.answer: Indicative content: Hazard management cycle; Park model stages - relief, rehabilitation, reconstruction; local vs international actors; contrasting examples (Haiti 2010, Christchurch 2011, Nepal 2015).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Placing a building on flexible bearings (rubber and steel pads) so that the ground can move without transferring all shaking to the structure"?
items.answer: base isolation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of base isolation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "recovery"?
options: Insurance that pays out automatically when a measured trigger (e.g. a magnitude or wind speed) is reached, rather than after loss assessment
The restoration of services, livelihoods and infrastructure after a disaster, over months to years
The period after an earthquake within which most trapped survivors can be rescued alive
Measuring seismicity, ground deformation, gas emissions and temperature to forecast eruptions
items.answer: The restoration of services, livelihoods and infrastructure after a disaster, over months to years
items.markingKey: B. "recovery" is the restoration of services, livelihoods and infrastructure after a disaster, over months to years.

items.stem: Which Sendai Framework priority focuses on "build back better"?
items.answer: Priority 4: enhancing preparedness for effective response and reconstruction
items.markingKey: Priority 4: enhancing preparedness for effective response and reconstruction. There are four priorities in total.

items.stem: "Earthquake early warning systems predict earthquakes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They detect earthquakes that have already started and give seconds of warning before strong shaking arrives.
items.markingKey: They detect earthquakes that have already started and give seconds of warning before strong shaking arrives. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how the Park model can be used to compare disaster responses.
items.answer: It plots quality of life over time through relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction; comparing curves shows how deep the impact was, how fast recovery occurred and whether conditions were improved after the disaster.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It plots quality of life over time through relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction; comparing curves shows how deep the impact was, how fast recovery occurred and whether conditions were improved after the disaster. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between resistance and resilience.
items.answer: Resistance is the ability to withstand a hazard without damage; resilience includes the ability to absorb impacts and recover quickly afterwards.
items.markingKey: Resistance is the ability to withstand a hazard without damage; resilience includes the ability to absorb impacts and recover quickly afterwards. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between protection and prediction.
items.answer: Prediction tries to forecast when and where a hazard will occur so people can be warned; protection reduces damage when it occurs, e.g. by building design or sea walls.
items.markingKey: Prediction tries to forecast when and where a hazard will occur so people can be warned; protection reduces damage when it occurs, e.g. by building design or sea walls. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between long-term recovery and emergency response.
items.answer: Emergency response happens in the first hours to weeks and focuses on saving lives and meeting basic needs; long-term recovery takes months to years and rebuilds housing, infrastructure and livelihoods.
items.markingKey: Emergency response happens in the first hours to weeks and focuses on saving lives and meeting basic needs; long-term recovery takes months to years and rebuilds housing, infrastructure and livelihoods. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how insurance increases resilience to geophysical hazards.
items.answer: It spreads losses across many people and over time, providing money for rapid rebuilding and reducing the economic burden on households and governments; risk-based premiums can encourage safer building.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It spreads losses across many people and over time, providing money for rapid rebuilding and reducing the economic burden on households and governments; risk-based premiums can encourage safer building. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: At a station in Kathmandu, the S-waves from an earthquake arrived 47.5 s after the P-waves. Assuming P-waves travel at 7.0 km/s and S-waves at 4.0 km/s, calculate the distance to the earthquake focus (d = Δt × vp × vs / (vp − vs)).
items.markingKey: M1 substitution; A1 443 km.

items.stem: The 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes (Mw 7.8 and 7.5) caused about 53,500 deaths in Türkiye (national population about 85 million); the 2010 Maule earthquake, Chile (Mw 8.8) caused about 525 deaths in Chile (population about 17.1 million). Calculate deaths per million people for each event. Suggest two reasons for the difference.
items.answer: Türkiye: 629.4 per million; Chile: 30.7 per million; higher: the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquakes (Mw 7.8 and 7.5); e.g. building codes and enforcement, poverty and informal construction, preparedness and warning systems, governance and emergency response, depth/distance of the earthquake from population.
items.markingKey: M1 deaths ÷ population (millions); A1 629.4; A1 30.7. R1 R1 two valid, developed reasons.

items.stem: Between 2005 and 2017 the annual insured losses from earthquakes recorded by a New Zealand public insurer changed from 2,767 to 2,288 US$ million. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (2,288 − 2,767) ÷ 2,767 × 100; A1 -17.3% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: The 2025 Mandalay earthquake, Myanmar had a moment magnitude of 7.7 and the February 2011 Christchurch earthquake, New Zealand had a magnitude of 6.2. Calculate how many times more energy was released by the first earthquake (energy increases by a factor of about 10^1.5 ≈ 31.6 per unit of magnitude).
items.answer: Energy ratio = 10^(1.5 × 1.5) ≈ 178 times

items.stem: The number of people living within 10 km of Mount Merapi, Indonesia was 157,796 people in 1995 and 175,110 people in 2005. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (175,110 − 157,796) ÷ 157,796 × 100; A1 +11.0% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem: The 2010 Maule earthquake, Chile (Mw 8.8) caused about 525 deaths in Chile (national population about 17.1 million); the 2010 Haiti earthquake (Mw 7.0) caused about 160,000 deaths in Haiti (population about 10.0 million). Calculate deaths per million people for each event. Suggest two reasons for the difference.
items.answer: Chile: 30.7 per million; Haiti: 16,000.0 per million; higher: the 2010 Haiti earthquake (Mw 7.0); e.g. building codes and enforcement, poverty and informal construction, preparedness and warning systems, governance and emergency response, depth/distance of the earthquake from population.
items.markingKey: M1 deaths ÷ population (millions); A1 30.7; A1 16,000.0. R1 R1 two valid, developed reasons.

items.stem: Briefly describe the Mount Vesuvius red zone, Italy and explain what it reveals about hazard mapping and zoning.
items.answer: About 700,000 people live in the red zone, with an evacuation plan and incentives to move. Mapping informs evacuation planning where relocation is politically difficult.
items.markingKey: Context (About 700,000 people live in the red zone, with an evacuation plan and incentives to move.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mapping informs evacuation planning where relocation is politically difficult. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to hazard mapping and zoning.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Post-event responses are less effective than pre-event strategies in reducing the impacts of geophysical hazards."
items.answer: Pre-event strategies are more cost-effective, but effective response and recovery remain essential.
items.markingKey: For: prevention saves more lives (codes, warnings). Against: rapid response saves trapped survivors. items.stem: To what extent do you agree that insurance is the most effective way to build resilience to geophysical hazards?
items.answer: Insurance builds financial resilience but must be combined with preparedness and risk reduction.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: speeds recovery (Christchurch); risk pooling (CCRIF). Against / limitations: does not save lives; unaffordable for the poor; community preparedness and codes matter more. A supported conclusion might be: Insurance builds financial resilience but must be combined with preparedness and risk reduction. items.stem:
Study the infographic / visual stimulus described below.

Table: building damage in a 2010s earthquake by construction type - unreinforced masonry: 62% collapsed; non-ductile concrete frame: 31%; reinforced concrete to modern code: 4%; timber frame: 2%.

(a) How many times more likely to collapse were unreinforced masonry buildings than modern reinforced concrete? [4]
(b) Using the resource and your own knowledge, explain the differences shown. [6]
items.answer: (a) 62 / 4 = 15.5 times (b) Unreinforced masonry is heavy and brittle; modern code concrete and timber are ductile and flex without collapsing.
